listenings.text: I am going to say something my colleagues will not thank me for. When I tell a supplier at the end of a meeting that this is really interesting and we will circle back, I have already decided, and the decision is no. It is not dishonesty, or at least it does not feel like it from this side. It is that saying no in the room to somebody who has flown a long way feels brutal, and the phrase gives everybody a soft exit. The people who work with us a lot know it perfectly well. What a yes sounds like is completely different, and the giveaway is that it is specific. If I am interested I will ask you for something before you leave the building. A sample, a reference, a date, anything. So the test is not whether I was warm, because I am always warm, it is whether I asked you for something. And if you want my honest advice, when you hear circle back, ask what the next step is and who owns it. Half the time you will simply be told, and the other half the silence answers the question.

The complaint I hear from clients about their foreign counterparts is almost always the same word, which is blunt, and the interesting thing is that it is never about rudeness. Nobody is being rude. What has happened is that a sentence has arrived without the layer that would normally sit on top of it. If I say we cannot deliver in June, that is a wall. If I say we may have to revisit June, it is the same fact with a door in it, and the other side can now move without anybody losing anything. Non-native speakers often build the sentence correctly and leave that layer off entirely, and the effect is that they sound more certain and more final than they are, which costs them a great deal in a negotiation. The fix is not more vocabulary. It is four or five modal patterns used until they are automatic. I would rather. It might well be. We may have to. They are bound to. Somebody who can produce those under pressure sounds like an insider, whatever their accent is.

reading.rtitle: What People Say When They Mean No
paras: A supplier flies eleven hours for a meeting, the meeting goes well, everybody is warm, and at the end the buyer says that this is really interesting and that they will circle back. The supplier flies home and tells his team it went well, because by every signal he knows how to read, it did. Six weeks later nobody has circled back and he does not understand what changed. Nothing changed. He was told no in the room and did not hear it, because in that room a no is almost never a word.

English-speaking business culture, and North American business culture in particular, marks refusal by temperature rather than by content. The vocabulary stays positive and the enthusiasm drops. Interesting is a warning. We would need to look at that internally is a decline. Let me take that away and think about it, unaccompanied by a date, means the thinking has already happened. Meanwhile a genuine yes is loud and specific and comes with a next step attached, usually before you have asked for one. The rule that experienced exporters use is simple: judge the meeting by what was agreed, not by how it felt.

There is a second half to this, which is harder, and it is that the same register is expected of you. A flat no is heard as aggressive and a flat yes is heard as unconsidered, so the language has an entire layer built for standing somewhere in between: we may have to, that might well be, I would rather, they are bound to. Foreign speakers who never acquire that layer are read as blunt, which is not what they are, and their sentences arrive with more force than they intended. Learning to hear the hedge and learning to use it are the same skill, approached from two directions.
